title: In Front of You
subtitle: Two buildings, one wall, and a voice that has said the same thing four hundred times.
escapeBrief:
The two players are friends that work in adjacent buildings: a museum and a cafe with a shop. The museum is currently showing historic weavings alongside their Jacquard card chains and the shop is selling replica weavings to tourists and museum goers. However, the pair has learned that one display in the museum is actually a fake. They need time alone in their respective buildings to prove the crime: to figure out which is the fake and where the original is, so they allow themselves to be locked in after hours. 

Under ultraviolet, natural dyes fluoresce and synthetic dyes do not. There is a UV light in the cafe/shop. The museum player needs the ultraviolet lamp, which starts in the shop and is useless there because everything in a shop is new. The cafe/shop also has a working loom, which can make weavings from Jacquard card chains. The shop player needs the Jacquard card chains, which start in the museum and are useless there because a museum loom is a conserved object and does not run.

The players move things between the buildings through a dumbwaiter that exists because the cafe caters museum events; it is not signposted, and noticing it is a channel is part of the puzzle. Nothing syncs - a docket code is read aloud and typed in by the other player. The museum player uses the UV lamp to inspect the seven display cases. Three cases show weavings with some dim spots - small amounts of modern material, because the museum once repaired a batch of pieces in one conservation campaign using the same modern thread. Three are bright - originals. One is dead across the whole field, and its identification card - printed recently, so full of optical brighteners - blazes while every genuine card stays dark. Meanwhile, the shop player runs a known-good chain first as a control, proving the loom is faithful, then runs the suspect chain. What it weaves does not match what is in the case; it matches a weaving on the shop's own shelf - the location of the missing original. On the selvedge of that original, there is a series of letters - the weaver's code. There is a similar code on all things for sale in the shop. However, entering that code into a keypad on each exterior door of the two buildings disarms security, allowing the players to escape to the street and meet each other.

The mill is UNLIT: every one of its windows is black, no lamp, bulb, candle or glow shows anywhere behind any of its glass, and no light falls on its brickwork at all. The chimney is a black silhouette with no light on it and nothing lit on its length. The panel of pavement lights is DARK: its lenses are wet and blank, with no light coming up through them and no glow from below. The lighting cabinet is set INTO the brickwork of the quoin, flush with it, with solid brick all round it, and its two isolator levers are BOTH DOWN and both in the same position as one another. Nothing stands in front of the lighting cabinet: the street lamp's standard is clear of it and does not cross it. There are EXACTLY 2 levers in the cabinet, EXACTLY 1 street lamp in the whole panorama -- the sodium standard on the corner, with no other lamp, lantern, bulb or lit fitting anywhere and in particular none on the mill -- EXACTLY 1 boarded gate in the lane, EXACTLY 1 shopfront, and EXACTLY 1 door in the mill's elevation. Every one of them is SHUT: no door, gate or opening anywhere in this picture stands open, ajar, lit from within, or shows anything at all of an interior behind it. The main street and the side lane are the only two ways the ground runs out of the frame; there is no third street, alley, ginnel, arch, passage, stair, step or opening anywhere, and no vehicle of any kind. The ONLY thing anywhere in this picture that can be operated is the lighting cabinet and its two levers: there is no keypad, keyboard, panel, dial, button, bell-push, handle plate, card reader or fitting of any kind on the mill's street door, on its jamb or brickwork, on the boarded gate or beside it, or anywhere else in the frame. The rain falls everywhere in the open and is visible only where the lamplight catches it. There are no people anywhere in this picture, and no part of a person. No legible lettering, numerals, captions, signage or text on any surface: printed cards, labels and tickets all appear as blank or wholly illegible shapes, and any woven mark is clearly present as a small uniform block on the cloth but its letters are not readable. The image is SHARP: no motion blur, no streaking, no smeared or doubled detail anywhere; everything in this picture is standing still, and any movement described is what the cinemagraph will add later, never something painted into the still.

lit.constraints: NOTHING has moved or changed position: the same corner from the same viewpoint, the same mill, chimney, shopfront, cabinet, lamp standard, gate, lane and town, all exactly where they are in the base scene, and it is still night and still raining hard. What changes is ONLY the light on the building. The two isolator levers in the open cabinet are now BOTH UP, and nothing else about the cabinet is different. THE BUILDING IS LIT FROM OUTSIDE, NOT FROM INSIDE: every window in the mill is still black behind its glass, with no lamp, bulb or glow anywhere within the building -- the floodlighting washes the brickwork and the glass reflects it, and that is all. No floodlight fitting, lamp head, bracket, cable or tripod is visible anywhere in the frame; only the light they throw. The mill's street door stays CLOSED and flush in the elevation exactly as in the base scene, its fanlight dark, and the floodlight washes over it without opening it or revealing anything behind it. There is still EXACTLY 1 street lamp in the whole frame -- the sodium standard on the corner -- and EXACTLY 1 boarded gate in the lane, still shut. No new door, gate, arch, passage, opening or lamp appears anywhere, and nothing that was shut is now open. The two buildings still stand in one continuous frontage with no gap between them. There are no people anywhere in this picture, and no part of a person.
lit.soundBed: a wet stone street corner in the open air at night, with a hill falling away below it: rain hissing off flagstones and slate, water running in the gutters, wind coming round the corner in gusts, the whole town quiet beyond -- and, once, the dull clack of heavy contactors closing somewhere in the brickwork.

rooms.designNote: [the corner · both | ESCAPE FINISH] THE FINALE, and the ONLY room both players reach. Exterior, on the corner where the mill's main street meets the warehouse's side lane — the payoff §13c chose over two doors facing each other. The mill has been a black void from the street all night and near-black inside at fifty lux, and the only sight either player has had of the other is one small rooflight across the yards. THE HERITAGE LIGHTING CABINET on the corner is the escape finish: throw it and the block's facade floodlighting strikes, and the thing they have been inside all night is seen whole for the first time — four storeys, the chimney, the garret's glazed band, the shop's front, and the party wall running between them. It is an ordinary grey steel cabinet in the brick that nobody ever looks at, which is the same register as the dumbwaiter being furniture. TERMINAL: no doors lead out of this room.

story:
You and your friend work either side of one wall — one of you in the textile museum, the other in the cafe and shop next door. Between you, you have worked out that one of the seven weavings on display in the museum is not the original, but you cannot prove it with the public in your spaces. So, tonight you have both let yourselves be locked in so that you have the time and privacy needed to gather evidence of this potential crime. You have until morning, and so does the evidence: the museum's seven pieces are a loan and the crates are collected at eight, and the shop's shelf stock is boxed for a trade fair the same morning. Once both lots leave the street, nothing you find tonight can be shown to anyone.

Start by solving the puzzles in your respective spaces: the museum has audio guide text — the stops on the permanent gallery, rewritten by eight different people over the years, and the shop has the menu — the kitchen's card box, eight different chefs, every dish written to one house formula. Work out how to tell one author from another, and be sure to discuss aloud how that analysis works. Then, turn those same analytical principles loose on the seven weavings: which display is the fake, and where did the original go? Answer both and you will have what you need to let yourselves out, one onto the main street and one into the side lane, and meet on the corner.

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster, square, seen flat and square-on: the bold black silhouette of a single deep hanging loop of laced Jacquard pattern cards — one broad ribbon of punched pasteboard falling in a single heavy loop — against a deep blue-black ground, with one warm amber glow behind it so the punched holes read as a scatter of small bright points burning through the dark ribbon. Two or three elements only, hard high contrast, graphic and poster-like, no gradients except the amber glow behind the loop. No people, no lettering, no text, no letters, no numbers, no border. Must read at thumbnail size.

ladderPlain.text: Museum. You grouped a pile of writing by which word came next, counted every pair, and read the single commonest continuation of a given word straight off the count.
Shop. Your partner did the same four steps on a different pile of writing, starting with the same count of which word followed which.
Museum. You fed the likeliest continuation back in as the new context and repeated it, and the chain settled into a short loop it could not leave.
Shop. The same chaining settled into a much shorter loop, three words long, running through a full stop — because punctuation was one of the tokens you counted.

Museum. You lengthened the context from one word to several and measured how much of it the writing still supported, finding the first length at which the model was resting on something it had seen exactly once.

Shop. The same measurement on the other pile gave a much smaller number. The two numbers are the point: how long a context a model can carry is a property of the writing it was built from, not of the model.
Museum. You generated forward at that length and compared the passage against each of the eight writers. It belonged to one of them, word for word.

Shop. The same generation on the other pile came back to one of the eight chefs, word for word. At that length the model is no longer choosing the next word; it is repeating a line it has only one record of.

Then you did it to an object instead of a sentence. You made a machine produce a pattern again in front of you, compared what it produced against what was on show, and traced the difference to the one thing in the building that carried it.

worldPlatePrompt: A world-bible establishing plate: ONE single continuous interior, a single unbroken photographic frame — NOT a grid, NOT a montage, NOT a contact sheet, NOT panels or tiles. The long ground floor of an old English silk mill on a wet winter night, looked down in one view from a conserved end to a working end. NEAREST THE VIEWER, THE CONSERVED END, AND IT IS DIM: worn grey stone flags, limewashed plaster and soot-dark brick under blackened timber trusses and black-painted cast-iron columns, a stretch of matt dark-grey exhibition wall, and one glazed display case lit from within by a single small warm lamp in a tight pool with deep shadow all round it. FURTHER DOWN, THE WORKING END, AND IT IS PLAINLY AND EVENLY BRIGHT: the same building turns busy, used and warmly cluttered — bare scrubbed boards and worn red quarry tile, honey-coloured timber shelving stacked with folded and rolled cloth, cream paint and scuffed deep-green tongue-and-groove panelling, oxblood-painted cast-iron columns, galvanised steel racking, white acid-free tissue, buff pasteboard pattern cards laced into long chains, waxed timber, a brass till, copper, brown paper and stacked crates, and a few small round tables with bentwood chairs pushed in under them, all under white enamel pendant shades hung low on long flex that light this end right into its corners. Tall small-paned cast-iron windows down one side show black wet night with rain running on the outside of the glass. The ONLY saturated colour anywhere is woven silk — madder red, indigo, gold, plum and deep blue — against an otherwise low warm-neutral palette of whitewash, worn stone, honey board, black and oxblood iron and grey brick. Kept and in daily use: nothing ruined, no rubble, no decay, no cobwebs. Warm and cluttered throughout, never clinical, never scrubbed, never laboratory-like. Painterly, cinematic, high contrast, fine film grain. LUX-NEUTRAL BY CONSTRUCTION: this one frame shows BOTH of this world's light levels at once — a tight warm pool in deep shadow at the conserved end, and plain even working brightness at the other — so the plate asserts neither as the default and each room's own prompt drives how dark or bright it is. No violet, ultraviolet or fluorescent light of any kind. No people, no figures, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage, no numbers.

done.title: Whose hand, and where it went
done.body: The model that sounded best had stopped composing and started copying, and the moment it did it named the hand it had learned. You turned the same reading on the seven, and the seven answered: one case dead under the lamp with its identification card blazing, and the original itself on the shop's own shelf, priced as a replica. You each hold half a case, and neither half is worth anything alone — which is why you spent the night talking through a hatch in a wall.

escapeDone.title: The corner, before eight
escapeDone.body: Five letters off a selvedge, typed into two keypads either side of one wall. The mill's street door lets one of you out onto the main street and the yard gate lets the other out into the side lane, and you come round the corner from opposite directions and meet on it in the rain. Behind you the crates are still stacked for eight o'clock — but the condition report will not be signed now, and the box going to the trade fair has one thing in it that was never a replica.
